client: I just failed my final calculus exam, and I can't stop thinking about it. It makes me question if I'm even cut out for this engineering major. Maybe I'm just not smart enough to handle the coursework like everyone else seems to be.
therapist: I hear how deeply this exam result has shaken your confidence, and it makes sense that you’d question your abilities right now. It sounds like this one setback is making you doubt your whole path—can you think of any past challenges in your coursework that you’ve overcome, even if they felt tough at the time?

client: I did manage to pass physics last semester after really struggling with it at first. But calculus feels different - when I see classmates breezing through problems I can't solve, it makes me feel like I'm fundamentally lacking something. Like I'm just not wired right for this.
therapist: It sounds like you're comparing your struggles to others' successes in a way that makes you feel defective—that "wired wrong" thought must be really painful. Since you pushed through physics successfully, what do you think helped you persist then that might apply to calculus now, even if it feels harder?

client: When I got through physics, I had a study group that really helped break things down. But with calculus, everyone seems to already understand the material, so I feel too embarrassed to ask questions or admit I’m struggling. It’s like I’m just falling further behind and can’t catch up.
therapist: I hear that shame about asking questions is keeping you from getting the help that worked for you before—that isolation must make the struggle feel even heavier. What do you think would happen if you reached out to just one classmate or the professor, even if it feels scary right now?

client: I guess I'm afraid they'll think less of me if I ask for help. Like my professor will see me as one of those students who shouldn't be in the program. And my classmates all seem so confident - what if they judge me for not getting it when it seems obvious to them?
therapist: That fear of being judged as "not belonging" sounds really vulnerable—it makes complete sense you'd hesitate to reach out when those thoughts are so loud. I wonder if we could test that assumption: what evidence do you have about how this professor or classmates have actually responded to others asking for help?

client: Now that you mention it, I’ve seen the professor stay after class to explain concepts to other students, and he didn’t seem annoyed. And I think one classmate did ask me for help on a problem last week... but I still feel like it’s different for me. Like my struggle means I’m not cut out for engineering, but theirs is just a temporary thing.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is holding you to a different standard than others—that must feel so exhausting and unfair. Could we explore why you're giving those students the benefit of "temporary struggle" but seeing your own challenges as proof you don't belong? Where do you think that double standard might come from?

client: I think it’s because I’ve always been told I need to be perfect to succeed in engineering—that there’s no room for mistakes. So when I struggle, it feels like I’m failing in a way that others aren’t. But I know that’s probably not realistic... it’s just hard to let go of that pressure.
therapist: It sounds like that "must be perfect" belief has been weighing on you for a long time, making every challenge feel like a personal failure—even though you know intellectually that mistakes are part of learning. What would it feel like to imagine that struggling with calculus doesn’t mean you’re failing, but that you’re simply growing into the engineer you want to become?

client: It’s hard to reframe it that way because I’ve always seen struggle as a sign I’m not good enough. But I guess if I think about it, even successful engineers had to learn and grow at some point. Still, it feels risky to think that way—like I’ll lower my standards and end up failing for real.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between this old belief—that struggle means you're not good enough—and this new, scary possibility that growth requires some stumbling. That tension must feel unsettling. What would it look like to hold both ideas gently: acknowledging the difficulty while also allowing that this might just be part of your path forward?

client: I guess I’ve never really considered that struggle could be part of the process—it’s always felt like something to avoid at all costs. But even if I try to think that way, I’m worried I’ll just use it as an excuse to not push myself hard enough. It’s like I don’t trust myself to find the balance between growth and giving up.
therapist: I hear how conflicted you feel—wanting to embrace this new perspective but fearing it might lead to complacency. That self-doubt about finding balance sounds exhausting. What would it look like to experiment with this mindset shift in small ways, while still honoring your work ethic—maybe noticing when struggle leads to growth without judging yourself for it?

client: I could try noticing when I improve on problems that used to baffle me, instead of just focusing on what I still don’t get. But part of me thinks, "So what if I’m making small progress? Real engineers don’t struggle this much." It’s like my brain dismisses any evidence that doesn’t fit the "I’m not good enough" story.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is quick to dismiss any progress, as if it’s not "enough"—that must feel frustrating when you’re trying to shift your perspective. What do you think it would take for those small wins to feel meaningful, even if they don’t erase the challenges? Could we explore what "enough" progress might look like to you?

client: I don’t even know what "enough" progress would look like—I’ve always just chased perfection. Maybe if I could solve problems without constantly second-guessing myself? But that feels impossible right now, and the idea of setting smaller goals almost makes me anxious that I’m settling.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between that old pull toward perfection and this new, uncomfortable idea of progress—no wonder it feels unsettling. What if we reframed "smaller goals" not as settling, but as stepping stones that actually build the confidence to tackle bigger challenges? How might that shift feel for you?
